newsitem.title: GERMANY: FAST E.EUROPE ALUMINIUM SMELTER EXPANSION UNLIKELY.
newsitem.headline: FAST E.EUROPE ALUMINIUM SMELTER EXPANSION UNLIKELY.

text.p: Rapid expansion of Eastern European aluminium output was not likely even though producers were working to modernise plants and improve market access, speakers at a Metal Bulletin conference said.

The sector's image problems among customers and lenders have hampered its efforts to overhaul capacity and operations. But foreign participation in processing and sales was helping to overcome difficulties.

The Slovalco plant at Ziar nad Hrnonom in Slovakia demonstrated successful co-operation between the private sector and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), sales and marketing head Einar Selsaas told the conference.
The bank and Norsk Hydro Aluminium financed the building of a new 132,000 tonnes per year primary and secondary plant, where liquid metal quality and purity had met expectations.
Productivity was still low because of high worker numbers but the plant had overcome logistics difficulties by arranging rail transport until the year 2000 and enjoyed competitive wages.

"We had to work hard to persuade customers that we're in Europe and part of the western world," Selsaas said of the plant that hopes to sell billets and wire rod to Germany, Italy, Austria and former COMECON countries.
"But the order-intake at the cast house has been satisfactory and we expect to reach full capacity this year."

Nandor Sillinger, director of privatisation at Hungarian Aluminium Industrial Co, said primary aluminium output would not be expanded but quality would be upgraded. The company was also trying to set up stable alumina supplies from Russia.
A number of investment projects were underway downstream and Germany's VAW was constructing a cast house in Gyor.
Romania was inviting foreign investment to raise output at the primary smelter at former state firm S.C. ALRO SA to ultimately 225,000 tpy from 146,000 currently, general manager Gheorghe Dobra said.
EBRD was developing an alumina plant at a Russian smelter and an aluminium can producer in the Czech republic, said Tim Lupprian, the bank's head of client risk management.
